title: Control flow and truthiness
summary: Every Python object is either truthy or falsy, and `if x:` asks the object that question rather than comparing it to anything. Knowing which values are falsy (and that `0`, `""`, `[]` and `None` are all among them) is the difference between a guard that works and one that silently skips.
definition: Truthiness is the boolean value Python derives from an object when it is used in a condition: it calls `__bool__` if the type defines one, falls back to `len(obj) != 0` if the type defines `__len__`, and otherwise treats the object as true. `if`, `while`, `and`, `or`, `not`, comprehension filters and ternaries all go through this single rule.
purpose: Conditions are where correctness usually leaks. `if not value:` reads like "if the caller gave me nothing", but it also fires on `0`, `0.0`, `""`, `[]` and `False`, all of which are things a caller may legitimately mean. You learn truthiness so that you can write a guard that tests the thing you actually care about, and so that you can read someone else's guard and see which cases it swallows.

body.md:
A condition in Python is not a comparison. `if x:` does not ask whether `x` equals `True`; it asks `x` to describe itself as true or false, using a rule that is fixed by the language and overridable by the type:

1. If the type defines `__bool__`, that answer is used.
2. Otherwise, if the type defines `__len__`, the object is false when its length is zero.
3. Otherwise the object is true. Every user-defined class with neither method is therefore always truthy, including one whose every field is empty.

That third rule is why `if my_config:` on a plain object is not a check that the config was populated: it is a check that the object exists at all, and it will keep passing after you delete every field.

rows: `type(None).__bool__` returns false; the only value of its type
numeric zero of any type is false
a non-empty string is true regardless of its text
length is 1; the contents are never inspected
midnight was falsy before 3.5, a historical trap in old code
the fallback; always true, even when empty

body.title: `if not x:` and `if x is None:` are different questions
body.md:
Use `is None` when you mean "the caller did not supply this". Use `not x` when you mean "this is empty or zero, and I want to treat that the same as absent".

```python
def page(limit=None):
    limit = limit or 100          # bug: limit=0 becomes 100
    limit = 100 if limit is None else limit   # correct
```

The `or` idiom is common and usually fine for strings, but every time the sentinel and a legitimate falsy value differ, it is wrong. `0` for "no limit", `""` for "an intentionally blank label" and `False` for an explicitly disabled flag are all values users send.

body.caption: `and` and `or` return an operand, not a boolean
body.code:
print(0 or "fallback")     # 'fallback': or returns the first truthy operand
print("a" or "b")          # 'a': and stops as soon as it can decide
print([] and crash())      # []: the right side is never evaluated
print(bool([] and 1))      # False

# Chained comparisons evaluate the middle operand once.
x = 5
print(1 < x < 10)          # True, and equivalent to 1 < x and x < 10

body.md:
Short-circuiting is a control-flow feature, not an optimisation. `if rows and rows[0].ok:` is safe precisely because `rows[0]` is not evaluated when `rows` is empty; reordering those two operands turns a working guard into an `IndexError`. The same property makes `x is not None and x.startswith("/")` the standard way to test an optional value without a nested `if`.

Because `and`/`or` return one of their operands rather than a bool, they compose into value expressions: `name = supplied or default` and `timeout = override and float(override)`. The cost is that the result's type is the union of both sides, which is worth remembering when the value flows into something that type-checks.

body.title: Choosing a condition
steps: Name the question precisely: absent, empty, zero, or false? These are four different things.
If the question is "absent", write `is None`. Identity, not truthiness, and never `== None`.
If the question is "empty", `if not items:` is idiomatic and preferred over `len(items) == 0`, but only for real containers.
If the value could be `0` or `False` and that is meaningful, you must not use bare truthiness. Compare explicitly.
If the object is a custom class, check that it defines `__bool__` or `__len__` before relying on `if obj:`, otherwise you are testing nothing.

body.definition_md: A unique object used to mean "no value supplied", chosen because it can never collide with real data. `None` is the default sentinel, but when `None` is itself a legal argument you create your own: `_MISSING = object()`, then `if value is _MISSING:`. This is the standard escape from the falsy-default problem.

body.title: Where this bites in real systems
body.md:
Config loading and request validation, almost every time. A feature flag arrives as `False`, a `or` default flips it back to `True`, and the flag appears not to work, with no error and no log line. Retry counts of `0`, prices of `0.00`, empty-string names that the user deliberately cleared, and pagination cursors of `0` all fail the same way.

The defensive habit worth building: in any function that takes optional parameters, resolve defaults with `is None` unless you have consciously decided that empty and absent are the same thing.

components.name: __bool__
components.role: The type's own answer; must return a real bool.

components.name: __len__
components.role: Fallback when `__bool__` is absent: zero length means false.

components.name: short-circuit evaluation
components.role: `and`/`or` stop as soon as the result is determined, which makes guards safe.

common_errors.error: A falsy-but-valid argument is replaced by the default: `limit = limit or 100` turns `limit=0` into `100`.
common_errors.cause: `or` tests truthiness, and `0` is falsy. The code conflates "not supplied" with "supplied as zero".
common_errors.fix: `limit = 100 if limit is None else limit`. When `None` is also a legal value, use a private sentinel: `_MISSING = object()`.

common_errors.error: `if value == None:` passes a linter's eye but can be defeated by a class that overrides `__eq__`.
common_errors.cause: `==` is a method call the object controls; `is` compares identity and cannot be intercepted.
common_errors.fix: Always `is None` / `is not None`. `None` is a singleton, so identity is exactly the right test.

common_errors.error: `if config:` keeps returning true after every field is emptied, so a "has anything been set" guard never fires.
common_errors.cause: A user-defined class with neither `__bool__` nor `__len__` is unconditionally truthy.
common_errors.fix: Test the thing you mean (`if config.entries:`) or give the class a `__bool__`/`__len__` that says what emptiness means for it.

common_errors.error: `if x is True:` fails for a value of `1`, and `if flag == True:` succeeds for `1` and `1.0`.
common_errors.cause: `bool` is a subclass of `int`, so `True == 1` while `True is not 1`.
common_errors.fix: Write `if flag:`. Comparing to `True` adds no safety and introduces two ways to be wrong.

common_errors.error: A guard raises `IndexError` after someone tidied the condition into `if rows[0].ok and rows:`.
common_errors.cause: The reordering removed the short-circuit that made the subscript safe.
common_errors.fix: Keep the cheap existence test on the left. Order in `and`/`or` is semantic, not stylistic.

best_practices: Use `is None` for absence and bare truthiness for emptiness, and never let the two blur together in a defaults line.
Prefer `if not items:` to `if len(items) == 0:` for containers, but only when you know the value is a container and not possibly `None`.
Let `and`/`or` short-circuit do your nil-guarding instead of nesting `if` statements; put the cheapest, most defensive test first.
Give any class whose emptiness is meaningful an explicit `__bool__` or `__len__`, so `if obj:` means something to a reader.
When a falsy value is legal input, say so in the signature (`limit: int | None = None`) so the `is None` check is obviously deliberate.
Reach for a private `object()` sentinel the moment `None` becomes a value the caller may legitimately pass.
production_considerations: Optional booleans in request payloads are the single most common source of this bug: `enabled=False` and `enabled` absent must be distinguished at the parsing boundary, not deep inside a handler.
Falsy-default bugs do not raise, so they are invisible to error tracking. They surface as support tickets about a setting that 'does not save', which makes them expensive to diagnose.
`if response:` on an HTTP client object depends entirely on that library's `__bool__`; some make a 404 falsy. Test the status code you care about instead of trusting the object.
In hot loops, truthiness on a large container is O(1) because `__len__` is O(1) for built-in types, but on a generator there is no length, so `if gen:` is always true and consumes nothing.
anti_patterns: `value = value or default` in any function that accepts numbers, booleans or strings that may legitimately be empty.
`if x == None`, `if x is True`, `if bool(x) == True`: three ways of writing `if x:` badly.
`if len(x) > 0:` where `x` may be `None`, which trades a silent skip for an `AttributeError` without fixing the ambiguity.
Relying on `if obj:` for a dataclass or plain class as a populated check, when no `__bool__` was ever defined.

examples.title: Resolving defaults without swallowing zero
examples.code:
_MISSING = object()

def fetch(limit=None, cursor=_MISSING):
    # limit=0 must survive; None means 'not supplied'.
    limit = 100 if limit is None else limit
    # None is a legal cursor value here, so None cannot be the sentinel.
    if cursor is _MISSING:
        cursor = load_last_cursor()
    return limit, cursor
